The problem: your bill has a charge even when you used almost no water

You did not water the lawn. You were out of town. The usage on your bill looks tiny. And yet there it is: a water "service charge," "base charge," "customer charge," or "meter charge."

That moment is frustrating because it feels like you are paying for nothing. You are not paying for nothing, but you also should not have to guess what the fee means. This guide explains what the fixed fee is, what it pays for, and how to sanity-check it.

If you want the big picture of how water bills are built (fixed fees + usage + sewer), start with our pillar: Water Service Explained.

  • What a water service charge is (and what it is not)
  • What the fixed fee usually covers
  • What real utility fixed charges look like (2026)

The quick answer

A water service charge is the fixed monthly fee that appears on your bill whether you used almost no water or a lot — it does not change with the gallons on the meter. It exists because the costs of keeping you connected — the meter, the bill, the mains held ready — don't shrink when you conserve; utilities structure bills as a fixed charge based on meter size plus a consumption charge based on use. [3][4] What you can lower is the usage charge: the per-unit part, billed in units like CCF (1 CCF = 748 gallons) or thousand gallons. [1]

What a water service charge is (and what it is not)

The fixed fee goes by different names:

  • Service charge
  • Base charge
  • Customer charge
  • Meter charge
  • Minimum charge (sometimes)

The key idea is not the label. The key idea is what it does: it is not a measurement of water you used. Your usage is measured separately, usually in gallons or CCF — one CCF equals 748 gallons. [1] If you keep seeing "CCF" on your bill and want to translate it into something you can picture, see: what CCF means on a water bill.

What the fixed fee usually covers

Think of the fixed fee as the cost of having an active account and a working connection. Even if your usage is low, the system still exists for you. Cleveland Water describes its two components plainly: "A fixed charge, based on the size of your water meter, and a consumption charge, based on how much water you use," with rate revenue funding "water main replacement projects" and "smart meters" as well as treatment plants. [4]

What the fixed side is tied to, and what it helps cover, commonly includes:

  • Meter costs (the meter itself, testing, replacement) [4]
  • Billing and customer service (statements, payment processing)
  • Operations and maintenance (mains, valves, pumps) [4]
  • Readiness costs (the system is sized and staffed so water is there when you open the tap)

Some utilities also list separate fixed fees for "fire line," "hydrant," or "infrastructure." Those are still fixed-fee ideas, just broken into multiple lines.

What real utility fixed charges look like (2026)

Fixed charges are set locally, and the spread is wide. Three municipal utilities, from their own current rate schedules:

  • Louisville Water Company (KY) — monthly service charge of $17.82 for a 5/8" or 5/8"x3/4" meter, $38.24 for 1", and $122.37 for 2", per its 2026 tariff effective January 1, 2026; the commodity charge is tiered at $1.70 per 1,000 gallons for the first 2,000 gallons and $4.70 for the next 8,000. [2]
  • Philadelphia Water Department (PA) — monthly water service charge of $5.96 for a 5/8" meter, $9.28 for 1", and $21.55 for 2", effective September 1, 2025. The regulation states plainly: "Water charges shall consist of a service charge and quantity charge," and "the type and size of the meter shall determine the service charge." [3]
  • Cleveland Water (OH) — monthly fixed charge of $9.90 in 2026 for the common residential 5/8"–1" meter, and $19.45 for 1 1/2"–2" meters, on a multi-year schedule that lists each year through 2029. [4]

Notice the pattern all three share: same city, bigger meter, bigger fixed charge — before a single gallon is counted. A larger meter can deliver more water at once, costs more to install and maintain, and its fixed charge is set higher to match. Philadelphia even has a process for customers who discover they are "over-metered" and can apply for a smaller meter and the lower charge that comes with it. [2][3]

Where to find the service charge on your bill

The service charge usually appears in a mini-itemized list. Look for a line that:

  • Is the same amount each month, or
  • Mentions "base," "service," "customer," or "meter," and
  • Does not change when your gallons or CCF change

If sewer rides on the same statement, don't be surprised if it looks bigger than the water service charge — sewer is often the larger of the two. That's covered in how sewer charges work.

How to sanity-check the charge

You don't need to be a rates expert to do a basic check:

1) Confirm it is fixed (not usage-based)

Compare two bills with different usage. If the line item stays the same, it is a fixed fee.

2) Check whether the charge scales with meter size

Many utilities tie the service charge to meter size — Louisville's schedule runs from $17.82 at 5/8" to $122.37 at 2" in the residential-to-small-commercial range alone. [2] Check which size appears on your bill.

3) Make sure you are not seeing "two fixed fees" that are actually different

Many "water bills" are two services on one statement: a water fixed charge plus a sewer base fee. Look for the headings that separate "Water" and "Sewer." If your total jumped and you're hunting the cause, start here: why your water bill suddenly increased.

What you can (and cannot) lower

This is the part most people care about, so let's be direct.

You can usually lower

  • Usage charges by reducing gallons/CCF (fix leaks, adjust irrigation, shorten showers)
  • Summer spikes by focusing on outdoor use

You usually cannot lower

  • The base/service charge without an account or meter-size change

Two practical next reads: if you suspect a hidden leak, use your meter as a truth source (water meter leak indicator explained); if the bill climbs every summer, the pattern is usually outdoor use plus tiered pricing (why water bills are higher in summer).

Common misconceptions

  • "The service charge means they estimated my usage." No. Estimated usage is about meter reads. The service charge is a fixed fee.
  • "If I used zero water, I should pay zero." It feels fair, but utility costs split into fixed system costs plus variable usage costs — and bills are structured the same way. [3][4]
  • "The fixed fee is the same everywhere." It is not: $5.96 a month in Philadelphia versus $17.82 in Louisville for the same 5/8" meter. [2][3]

Next steps if it still feels wrong

  1. Confirm the account status (active vs vacant vs seasonal). Some cities have special rates for vacant properties.
  2. Confirm meter size. If the fixed fee is tied to meter size, make sure the size on your bill matches what is actually installed — Philadelphia even runs a process for "over-metered" customers to downsize and drop to the lower charge. [3]
  3. Separate water vs sewer. Many "water bills" are really two services on one statement.

If the fixed charge jumped year over year, check your utility's current rate schedule first — adopted rate increases (Cleveland's, for instance, are published year by year) explain most jumps, and a wrong meter size on the bill is a billing error worth disputing. [4]
